title: The use of social media in the creation political awareness of youth in Delta State
screen_reason: Cross-sectional questionnaire survey of 475 usable respondents in Delta State, Nigeria. Table 2 item 2 asks respondents to agree/disagree that 'Most political information on social media are false and unreliable', and the paper reports the agreeing share (N = 58%; SA 177 (37%) + A 97 (20%)). Under the protocol this is a RECALL measure of the perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment, reported as a share of respondents.

estimates.platform: Social media generally (Facebook 40.2%, WhatsApp 31.8%, Twitter 13.9%, Instagram 12.2%, YouTube 1.9%)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents agreeing that most political information on social media is false and unreliable
estimates.value_raw: N = 58% (Strongly Agree 177 (37%) + Agree 97 (20%) of 475; X = 3.4; SD = 1.5)
estimates.denominator: 475 Delta State residents who returned usable questionnaires (of 500 distributed, 95% response rate), all of whom use social media
estimates.definition: Respondent answered Strongly Agree or Agree to the Likert item 'Most political information on social media are false and unreliable'
estimates.misinfo_def: Most political information on social media are false and unreliable (the survey item itself; the paper gives no formal definition of misinformation)
estimates.source_quote: Table 2 showed that although the respondents identified the peculiar nature of social media political awareness to be false, unreliable (N =58%; X = 3.4; SD =1.5) ... [Table 2, item 2] Most political information on social media are false and unreliable | 177 (37) | 97 (20) | 13 (3) | 131 (28) | 57 (12) | 3.4 (1.5) | Accept
estimates.page_loc: Table 2 (item 2) and the paragraph immediately below it, p. 11
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report on a 5-point Likert scale (1 Strongly Disagree to 5 Strongly Agree); instrument content-validated by two experts, pilot Cronbach alpha .878.
estimates.moderator_quote: A multi stage sampling technique was used to select the respondents ... At the last stage, accidental sampling technique was used to select 50 respondents from each of the ten towns. Data were collected using a structured likert scale questionnaire with responses ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree).
estimates.notes: The 58% is the authors' own figure in the results text; the table's own cells give 37% + 20% = 57% and the raw counts 274/475 = 57.7%. The verbatim 58% is kept per R8 (a cross-category sum computed by the extractor would not be). Year is the publication year: no fieldwork date is given anywhere in the paper. Sampling frame coded survey_sample (multistage: stratified senatorial district, random LGAs and towns) although the final stage is accidental/convenience sampling, which weakens representativeness. Confidence held at medium because the paper is internally sloppy: the narrative below Table 2 quotes statistics that do not match the table it describes (e.g. 'trivial issues (N =52%; X = 3.1; SD =1.6)' against a table row showing X = 4.1), the first row of Table 3 is garbled, and several references appear to be find-and-replace artefacts ('Delta State Vision', 'Social Media, Newspapers and Political Awareness of Youth in Delta State'), suggesting the text was adapted from a study conducted elsewhere. The cell extracted here is however internally consistent (counts, percentages and mean all agree).

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: 'Political conversations on social media are often mundane, trivial' (78% agree) and 'Social media political awareness are generated by anyone and everyone' (74%) - not misinformation; the hate-speech item in Table 3 (hate speech is not misinformation); 'Political awareness found on the social media are never current and up to date' (86% disagree) - a currency judgement, not veracity. Exposure-frequency items (55.4% 'very often' exposed to social media) measure platform use, not misinformation exposure.

rob.design: Cross-sectional questionnaire survey, population 663,362 Delta State youth, sample 500 by multistage sampling (stratified senatorial district -> simple random LGAs and towns -> accidental sampling of 50 per town), 475 usable (95% response); 5-point Likert instrument, content validity by two experts, pilot Cronbach alpha .878; descriptive percentages, means and SDs; no fieldwork date reported.
